newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy leftist chief puts reform before government.
newsitem.headline: Italy leftist chief puts reform before government.

text.p: The leader of the largest party within the Italian centre-left coalition said on Wednesday the question of constitutional reform was more important than worries about the survival of the government.

Massimo D'Alema, head of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), is leading negotiations to set up a cross-party commission to work out a much needed reform of Italy electoral and parliamentary system.

However parties within Prime Minister Romano Prodi's coalition are divided amongst themselves over what kind of reform is needed, while the opposition centre-right says it wants written assurances before joining any commission.

The hardleft Communist Refoundation, which guarantees the government's majority in the lower house, has threatened to withdraw its support if the PDS sides with the centre-right over the reform issue.

"It would not be right to give in to blackmail from people who would bring down the government to prevent reforms," D'Alema told reporters at a book presentation attended by centre-right leader and former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi.
"If the centre-left does not carry out reforms, then its historical mission will have failed," he added. "The interest of the country should prevail over the interests of a government."

D'Alema and Berlusconi agreed at a meeting on Tuesday that talks over the planned parliamentary commission should be put off until parliament finishes examining the 1997 budget. The financial bill has to be passed into law by the end of the year.
The right wants to introduce a presidential-style government and hardright leader Gianfranco Fini has demanded a guarantee that the proposed commission will move in this direction.
Refoundation and other government supporters, including the centrist Popular Party, are opposed to such an electoral system.
However D'Alema said on Wednesday he was hopeful that reform would eventually be worked out.
"The left has a greater need of an efficient state than the right because we don't believe that all problems can be resolved by the market," he told reporters.
Politicians have talked for 15 years about the need to modernise Italy's 1948 constitution and end the history of revolving-door governments.

Many commentators believed that the huge corruption scandals at the start of the 1990s, which destroyed the old ruling elite, would usher in swift reform, but apart from some mild tinkering with the system, there have been no major changes.
